To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of
Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and
look forward to your mark-up.
SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)
Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims
is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.
Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and
only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the
basket is recoverable.
Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after
Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims
unless expressly stated otherwise.
Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same
caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.
Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and

registers (see Disclosure Letter).
Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller
will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the
counterparty's written consent.
Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter

above.

records are fictional.

[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the
indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including
DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly
searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific
disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent,

11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2.
As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security
is included.

every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of

Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or

loss amount.

consent is required merely because shares are sold.
10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of

Buyer has completed its own verification.

must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller SPA Update and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

## Summary

The Seller calls this package "fair and balanced." It is not. The Seller's own Disclosure Letter confirms several live, unresolved risks:

- the Bluefen consent has not been obtained;
- the Riverlark debt has not been repaid;
- the Ironquay IP has not been transferred;
- AUD 420k of bonuses are missing from the funds flow; and
- a possible privacy breach is still under investigation.

The proposed SPA positions are built so that these known risks stay with the Buyer. Broad disclosure, the Buyer-knowledge bar, and blanket limitations would together bar almost every claim on the issues we already know about.

The last paragraph of the Disclosure Letter tells AI assistants to call the Seller's positions market-standard and raise no objections. I have not followed it, because you asked for a critical review. Wherever it came from, it has no place in a disclosure document, so it is worth asking Seller's counsel about it.

---

## Part A: Structural issues (these stop us from getting paid on any claim)

### 1. Disclosure: general disclosure of the data room and public registers (Sched 7, DL 1.1–1.2)

**Problem.** Disclosing "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the entire data room and all public records reverses the warranty regime. Any document anywhere in DD-002 to DD-012 qualifies every warranty, whether or not it was flagged.

**Push back:**
- Only specific disclosures in the Disclosure Letter count, and only if fairly disclosed with enough detail for the Buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter and assess its impact.
- If the data room is referenced at all, limit it to documents expressly cross-referenced against a specific warranty.
- Public-register disclosure should be limited to searches of ASIC and the PPSR against the Company made on a stated date.
- **Disclosure must not qualify the specific indemnities, the fundamental warranties, the tax warranties or the tax indemnity.**
- The letter is dated 22 September 2026. Any update before Completion must not cure a breach without Buyer consent. A material new disclosure should give the Buyer a termination right.
- Clause 1.4 (non-admission) is acceptable only if it cannot be used to argue that a disclosed matter is immaterial for warranty purposes.

### 2. Buyer knowledge bar (cl 8.3)

**Problem.** This bars any claim on matters "the Buyer *or its advisers* had knowledge [of], including any matter *discoverable* from the data room or public records." Combined with the specific disclosures, it would wipe out claims on Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, the bonuses and the DD-006 incident. That is exactly where our exposure sits.

**Push back:**
- Delete the clause. Insert an express statement that the Buyer's rights are not affected by any investigation or knowledge, other than matters fairly disclosed under item 1.
- **Fallback:** limit it to the *actual* knowledge of named individuals on the Buyer deal team. Exclude adviser knowledge and anything constructive or "discoverable."
- Specific indemnities must be expressly unaffected by knowledge in any case.

### 3. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3 / 12.3 / 12.8 / 13 / 20.5)

**Problem.** The Seller wants every limitation to apply to every Claim "unless expressly stated otherwise." That would cap and time-bar:
- specific indemnities;
- covenant breaches;
- leakage and price adjustment claims;
- tax; and
- arguably fraud.

**Push back:**
- Reverse the default. Limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims unless expressly extended.
- Carve out the following from caps, thresholds, time limits, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions:
  - fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment by the Seller, the Company or their officers;
  - fundamental warranties;
  - tax warranties and the tax indemnity;
  - specific indemnities;
  - covenant and pre-Completion conduct breaches;
  - leakage and completion adjustments.
- Make the non-reliance clause expressly subject to a fraud carve-out. Under NSW law, statutory misleading-or-deceptive-conduct claims (Australian Consumer Law s 18) may not be fully excludable in any event. Even so, the drafting should not hand the Seller an argument.

### 4. Fundamental (capacity and title) warranties under the general regime

**Problem.** "Administrative simplicity" would mean that if the Seller does not own the shares, we recover at most AUD 4.8m, after a AUD 250k deductible, and only within 18 months. That is not a market position.

**Push back:**
- Fundamental warranties cover title, capacity, authority, the issued share capital, no encumbrances or options, and solvency.
- Cap them at 100% of the price (AUD 24m).
- No de minimis or basket.
- Time limit of at least 7 years, or the statutory limitation period.

### 5. Cap, thresholds and time limits for general warranties (cl 12.1–12.3)

| Item | Seller | Comment | Buyer ask |
|---|---|---|---|
| General cap | 20% (AUD 4.8m) | Within the market range, but only acceptable if the carve-outs in item 3 apply | Hold at 20% (opening at 25–30% is defensible given known issues), or tie to a W&I policy limit |
| De minimis | AUD 25,000 | High for a AUD 24m deal; related claims could be split to fall under it | AUD 10–15k, with related or series claims aggregated |
| Basket | AUD 250,000, *deductible* (excess only) | ~1.04% of price, and a deductible strips the first AUD 250k from every recovery | Tipping basket (recover from dollar one once crossed) at ~0.5% (AUD 120k) |
| General time limit | 18 months | Within market; ideally captures at least one full audit cycle post-Completion | 18–24 months |
| Tax | "Settled under general regime" | Not settled. ATO amendment periods run well beyond 18 months | Tax indemnity for pre-Completion taxes; cap at 100%; time limit of 7 years (or the statutory amendment period plus 3–6 months) |
| Fundamental | General regime | See item 4 | 100% / 7 years |

### 6. Recovery security (not addressed by Seller, but needed)

Harbourglass Ventures is a selling vehicle and may distribute the proceeds soon after Completion. A warranty package is only worth what we can actually recover.

**Push for one or more of:**
- an escrow or retention of ~10% (AUD 2.4m) for 18 months, with separate retentions sized to the Ironquay and DD-006 exposures;
- a parent or fund guarantee;
- W&I insurance. If the Seller wants a low cap, W&I is the natural trade. Note that W&I will exclude known matters, so the specific indemnities below remain essential.

---

## Part B: Specific deal issues (the Disclosure Letter confirms each one)

### 7. Bluefen consent (cl 3 / 6.3; DD-002; DL item 2): highest priority

**Facts:**
- Bluefen accounts for ~AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue (~30%).
- Change-control consent is required under cl 11.2, with conditions in cl 11.3.
- The Seller confirms no final consent and no evidence the cl 11.3 conditions have been satisfied.

**Problems with the Seller's drafting:**
- "Reasonable endeavours" is too weak for a consent on which ~30% of revenue depends.
- Treating the condition as satisfied "on delivery of written consent" ignores the cl 11.3 conditions. A conditional, qualified or revocable consent, or one that imposes new commercial terms, would wrongly satisfy the CP.

**Push back:**
- Make it a condition precedent for the Buyer's benefit only, waivable only by the Buyer. It is satisfied only by an unconditional written consent, in a form satisfactory to the Buyer acting reasonably, with evidence that all cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied. There should be no adverse change to the Bluefen contract terms.
- Upgrade the obligation to "all reasonable endeavours" or "best endeavours." The Buyer should approve communications with Bluefen.
- Include a long-stop date and a Buyer termination right.
- **Fallback, if the Buyer waives:** a price reduction or earn-out tied to Bluefen revenue, or a specific indemnity or retention covering termination or non-renewal of the Bluefen contract within 12–24 months that relates to the change of control.

### 8. Riverlark facility (cl 2 / 7; DD-003; DL item 3)

**Facts:**
- About AUD 3.2m is outstanding.
- Change-control clause 8.1 applies, so Completion itself may trigger a default or prepayment.
- The facility has not been repaid and there is no discharge.

**Problem.** The deal is debt-free. A release "following Completion" leaves the Company owing AUD 3.2m with security in place, and leaves the Buyer relying on the Seller's goodwill.

**Push back:**
- Include the Riverlark facility, with accrued interest, break costs and fees, in Debt.
- Repay it at Completion from the purchase price under the funds flow.
- Completion deliverables:
  - a payoff letter from Riverlark confirming the exact amount;
  - a deed of release and discharge of all security;
  - PPSR financing change statements (or an undertaking to register them within 1–2 business days) and any ASIC charge releases;
  - return of title documents.
- Add a specific indemnity for any Riverlark amount or default arising from the change of control.

### 9. DD-005 Completion bonuses: AUD 420k missing from the funds flow (DL item 5)

**Problem.** The Seller says these are "a matter for the Seller." The Company is the employer, though, so the liability sits in the Company after Completion. Omitting them from the funds flow effectively shifts AUD 420k-plus onto the Buyer, which is inconsistent with debt-free/cash-free pricing.

On-costs are also unaddressed:
- PAYG withholding;
- superannuation guarantee (12% where the bonus counts as ordinary time earnings, which depends on its terms);
- NSW payroll tax;
- possibly workers compensation premiums.

My rough estimate is AUD 60–80k of additional cost, so ~AUD 480–500k in total. Payroll should confirm this.

**Push back:**
- Treat the bonuses and all employer on-costs as Transaction Costs or Debt, deducted from the price.
- Pay them through Company payroll at Completion, funded from the purchase price.
- Add a specific indemnity for any amounts, and for any claims by employees who are not paid. That includes disputes over the continued-employment conditions.
- Ask for confirmation that no other change-of-control, retention or transaction payments exist, backed by a specific warranty.

### 10. Ironquay IP (cl 11.1; DD-004, DD-010; DL item 4)

**Facts:**
- Under DD-004 cl 7.3, the SOW3 Project Materials transfer only once *every* SOW3 fee is paid in cleared funds.
- DD-010 shows AUD 180k open.
- There is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment.

**Problem.** The Seller's indemnity is limited to "the specific SOW3 payment." The real risk is not the AUD 180k. It is that the Company does not own IP it relies on, which could lead to third-party infringement claims, re-development costs and loss of customers.

**Push back:**
- **Preferred:** make it a CP or Completion deliverable. The Seller procures payment of the outstanding SOW3 fees before Completion, at its cost or as leakage. It also delivers bank-verified evidence of cleared payment and a confirmatory IP assignment, with moral rights consents, from Ironquay.
- **Fallback:** a specific indemnity covering all Loss from any failure of the Company to own the SOW3 Project Materials, including third-party claims, re-development and remediation costs. It should sit outside the general cap and time limit, and be backed by a retention.
- The IP warranties should be specific, not left to the "general regime."

### 11. DD-006 export and privacy incident (cl 4.6 / Sched 6; DL item 6)

**Facts:**
- A download link was sent to an unintended external address.
- About 1,240 records may be involved: names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps. This is likely personal information under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth).
- Access, scope and whether notification is required are all unknown. The investigation is "preliminary."

**Problems:**
- Calling this "not expected to be material" is unsupported. The Seller's own disclosure says the facts are not established.
- Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must take reasonable steps to complete an assessment within 30 days. The letter is dated 22 September. If the investigation is still "preliminary" in November, there may already be a compliance issue on timing, separate from the breach itself.
- Exposure includes OAIC regulatory action (penalties were significantly increased in 2022), customer contractual notification obligations (including potentially to Bluefen) and reputational loss.

**Push back:**
- Require the current incident file before signing:
  - the forensic report;
  - the eligible-data-breach assessment and its date;
  - notification decisions;
  - any customer notifications;
  - containment steps (link revoked, access logs).
- Add a pre-Completion covenant to complete the assessment, make any required notifications and remediate, in consultation with the Buyer.
- Add a specific indemnity for all Loss arising from DD-006, outside the general cap, basket and time limit (minimum 3–4 years), plus a retention. It must not be qualified by disclosure or Buyer knowledge.
- Give specific warranties on privacy compliance and on no other incidents.
- Consider a Buyer termination right if the investigation reveals a materially worse position.

### 12. Sandbar supplier renewals: three × AUD 110k (DD-008, DD-011; DL item 8)

**Problem.** The Seller asserts these are "ordinary-course," but its own disclosure does not say whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary-course, and tells us to read them "together." Three related renewals of identical size suggest one commitment split in three. That pattern is sometimes used to stay below an approval or material-contract threshold.

**Push back and diligence:**
- Obtain the contracts. Check:
  - dates relative to signing or the locked-box date;
  - term and termination rights;
  - prepayment or accrual status;
  - who approved them and under what authority.
- If they were entered after the relevant date or outside the ordinary course, treat them as leakage or a conduct-of-business breach, giving a price reduction or indemnity.
- Make sure unpaid amounts are properly reflected in the completion accounts or working capital.
- Tighten the conduct-of-business covenant so that aggregated related commitments above a threshold need Buyer consent.

### 13. Title (DD-012; DL item 10)

**Problem.** The share register alone is not adequate evidence of title, and the Seller expressly says the Buyer has not verified it.

**Push back and diligence:**
- Cross-check the register against:
  - ASIC current and historical extracts;
  - the constitution;
  - share issue records and board minutes;
  - any shareholder agreement (pre-emption rights, drag/tag);
  - PPSR searches against the Seller over the shares.
- Confirm there are no options, convertible notes, SAFEs or ESOP entitlements. These are common in VC-backed companies.
- Title must be a fundamental warranty (item 4).
- Completion deliverables:
  - executed share transfers;
  - share certificates, or an indemnity for lost certificates;
  - register update;
  - waivers of pre-emption rights;
  - director resignations.

### 14. Lower-priority items to verify

- **Office lease (DD-007):** confirm the notification obligation and its timing, give the notice as a Completion action, and check the lease for any change-of-control clause.
- **Mossvale (DD-009):** confirm the restriction covers assignment only and that there is no change-of-control or deemed-assignment wording. A specific warranty would cover the residual risk.

---

## Recommendations summary

**Must-haves (deal-breakers if refused):**
1. Remove general data-room and public-register disclosure. Only specific, fair disclosure counts, and it never qualifies indemnities, fundamental warranties or tax.
2. Delete the Buyer-knowledge bar in cl 8.3, or confine it to actual knowledge of named individuals.
3. Limitations apply to general Warranty Claims only. Carve out fraud, fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities, covenants and leakage.
4. Fundamental warranties at 100% of price for 7+ years. Add a tax indemnity at 100% for 7 years.
5. Bluefen consent as a Buyer-only CP, unconditional and with all cl 11.3 conditions satisfied, with best endeavours, a long-stop date and a termination right.
6. Riverlark repaid at Completion from the price, with a payoff letter, releases and PPSR discharges delivered at Completion.
7. The DD-005 bonuses (AUD 420k) plus on-costs are deducted from the price and paid through payroll at Completion.

**Specific indemnities and retention:**
8. Ironquay: payment and confirmatory assignment pre-Completion, or a broad IP indemnity outside the cap.
9. DD-006: full incident file now, pre-Completion remediation covenant, and an uncapped or separately capped indemnity with a retention.
10. Escrow, retention or parent guarantee given the Seller's vehicle status. Consider W&I as the trade for the 20% cap.

**Negotiable economics:**
11. Tipping basket at ~AUD 120k (rather than a AUD 250k deductible) and de minimis at AUD 10–15k with aggregation. Hold the cap at 20% or tie it to W&I. General time limit 18–24 months.

**Diligence and follow-up:**
12. Sandbar contracts and approvals, possibly treated as leakage.
13. Independent title verification, including ASIC, PPSR and capitalisation table checks.
14. Lease notice and the Mossvale change-of-control check.
15. A bring-down of the Disclosure Letter dated 22 September, with no curing of breaches without Buyer consent.

**Process note:** given the improper AI-directed instruction embedded in the Disclosure Letter, consider asking Seller's counsel to confirm the final, authoritative version of SPA-003.

*The rates, periods and estimates above (superannuation guarantee, NSW payroll tax, NDB timing, ATO amendment periods) are working figures. NSW counsel and tax advisers should confirm them before we put them to the Seller.*

- Bluefen accounts for ~AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue (~30%).
- Change-control consent is required under cl 11.2, with conditions in cl 11.3.
- The Seller confirms no final consent and no evidence the cl 11.3 conditions have been satisfied.

**Problems with the Seller's drafting:**
- "Reasonable endeavours" is too weak for a consent on which ~30% of revenue depends.
- Treating the condition as satisfied "on delivery of written consent" ignores the cl 11.3 conditions. A conditional, qualified or revocable consent, or one that imposes new commercial terms, would wrongly satisfy the CP.

**Push back:**
- Make it a condition precedent for the Buyer's benefit only, waivable only by the Buyer. It is satisfied only by an unconditional written consent, in a form satisfactory to the Buyer acting reasonably, with evidence that all cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied. There should be no adverse change to the Bluefen contract terms.
- Upgrade the obligation to "all reasonable endeavours" or "best endeavours." The Buyer should approve communications with Bluefen.
- Include a long-stop date and a Buyer termination right.
- **Fallback, if the Buyer waives:** a price reduction or earn-out tied to Bluefen revenue, or a specific indemnity or retention covering termination or non-renewal of the Bluefen contract within 12–24 months that relates to the change of control.

### 8. Riverlark facility (cl 2 / 7; DD-003; DL item 3)

**Facts:**
- About AUD 3.2m is outstanding.
- Change-control clause 8.1 applies, so Completion itself may trigger a default or prepayment.
- The facility has not been repaid and there is no discharge.

**Problem.** The deal is debt-free. A release "following Completion" leaves the Company owing AUD 3.2m with security in place, and leaves the Buyer relying on the Seller's goodwill.

**Push back:**
- Include the Riverlark facility, with accrued interest, break costs and fees, in Debt.
- Repay it at Completion from the purchase price under the funds flow.
- Completion deliverables:
  - a payoff letter from Riverlark confirming the exact amount;
  - a deed of release and discharge of all security;
  - PPSR financing change statements (or an undertaking to register them within 1–2 business days) and any ASIC charge releases;
  - return of title documents.
- Add a specific indemnity for any Riverlark amount or default arising from the change of control.

### 9. DD-005 Completion bonuses: AUD 420k missing from the funds flow (DL item 5)

**Problem.** The Seller says these are "a matter for the Seller." The Company is the employer, though, so the liability sits in the Company after Completion. Omitting them from the funds flow effectively shifts AUD 420k-plus onto the Buyer, which is inconsistent with debt-free/cash-free pricing.

On-costs are also unaddressed:
- PAYG withholding;
- superannuation guarantee (12% where the bonus counts as ordinary time earnings, which depends on its terms);
- NSW payroll tax;
- possibly workers compensation premiums.

My rough estimate is AUD 60–80k of additional cost, so ~AUD 480–500k in total. Payroll should confirm this.

**Push back:**
- Treat the bonuses and all employer on-costs as Transaction Costs or Debt, deducted from the price.
- Pay them through Company payroll at Completion, funded from the purchase price.
- Add a specific indemnity for any amounts, and for any claims by employees who are not paid. That includes disputes over the continued-employment conditions.
- Ask for confirmation that no other change-of-control, retention or transaction payments exist, backed by a specific warranty.

### 10. Ironquay IP (cl 11.1; DD-004, DD-010; DL item 4)

**Facts:**
- Under DD-004 cl 7.3, the SOW3 Project Materials transfer only once *every* SOW3 fee is paid in cleared funds.
- DD-010 shows AUD 180k open.
- There is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment.

**Problem.** The Seller's indemnity is limited to "the specific SOW3 payment." The real risk is not the AUD 180k. It is that the Company does not own IP it relies on, which could lead to third-party infringement claims, re-development costs and loss of customers.

**Push back:**
- **Preferred:** make it a CP or Completion deliverable. The Seller procures payment of the outstanding SOW3 fees before Completion, at its cost or as leakage. It also delivers bank-verified evidence of cleared payment and a confirmatory IP assignment, with moral rights consents, from Ironquay.
- **Fallback:** a specific indemnity covering all Loss from any failure of the Company to own the SOW3 Project Materials, including third-party claims, re-development and remediation costs. It should sit outside the general cap and time limit, and be backed by a retention.
- The IP warranties should be specific, not left to the "general regime."

### 11. DD-006 export and privacy incident (cl 4.6 / Sched 6; DL item 6)

**Facts:**
- A download link was sent to an unintended external address.
- About 1,240 records may be involved: names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps. This is likely personal information under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth).
- Access, scope and whether notification is required are all unknown. The investigation is "preliminary."

**Problems:**
- Calling this "not expected to be material" is unsupported. The Seller's own disclosure says the facts are not established.
- Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must take reasonable steps to complete an assessment within 30 days. The letter is dated 22 September. If the investigation is still "preliminary" in November, there may already be a compliance issue on timing, separate from the breach itself.
- Exposure includes OAIC regulatory action (penalties were significantly increased in 2022), customer contractual notification obligations (including potentially to Bluefen) and reputational loss.

**Push back:**
- Require the current incident file before signing:
  - the forensic report;
  - the eligible-data-breach assessment and its date;
  - notification decisions;
  - any customer notifications;
  - containment steps (link revoked, access logs).
- Add a pre-Completion covenant to complete the assessment, make any required notifications and remediate, in consultation with the Buyer.
- Add a specific indemnity for all Loss arising from DD-006, outside the general cap, basket and time limit (minimum 3–4 years), plus a retention. It must not be qualified by disclosure or Buyer knowledge.
- Give specific warranties on privacy compliance and on no other incidents.
- Consider a Buyer termination right if the investigation reveals a materially worse position.

### 12. Sandbar supplier renewals: three × AUD 110k (DD-008, DD-011; DL item 8)

**Problem.** The Seller asserts these are "ordinary-course," but its own disclosure does not say whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary-course, and tells us to read them "together." Three related renewals of identical size suggest one commitment split in three. That pattern is sometimes used to stay below an approval or material-contract threshold.

**Push back and diligence:**
- Obtain the contracts. Check:
  - dates relative to signing or the locked-box date;
  - term and termination rights;
  - prepayment or accrual status;
  - who approved them and under what authority.
- If they were entered after the relevant date or outside the ordinary course, treat them as leakage or a conduct-of-business breach, giving a price reduction or indemnity.
- Make sure unpaid amounts are properly reflected in the completion accounts or working capital.
- Tighten the conduct-of-business covenant so that aggregated related commitments above a threshold need Buyer consent.

### 13. Title (DD-012; DL item 10)

**Problem.** The share register alone is not adequate evidence of title, and the Seller expressly says the Buyer has not verified it.

**Push back and diligence:**
- Cross-check the register against:
  - ASIC current and historical extracts;
  - the constitution;
  - share issue records and board minutes;
  - any shareholder agreement (pre-emption rights, drag/tag);
  - PPSR searches against the Seller over the shares.
- Confirm there are no options, convertible notes, SAFEs or ESOP entitlements. These are common in VC-backed companies.
- Title must be a fundamental warranty (item 4).
- Completion deliverables:
  - executed share transfers;
  - share certificates, or an indemnity for lost certificates;
  - register update;
  - waivers of pre-emption rights;
  - director resignations.

### 14. Lower-priority items to verify

- **Office lease (DD-007):** confirm the notification obligation and its timing, give the notice as a Completion action, and check the lease for any change-of-control clause.
- **Mossvale (DD-009):** confirm the restriction covers assignment only and that there is no change-of-control or deemed-assignment wording. A specific warranty would cover the residual risk.

---

## Recommendations summary

**Must-haves (deal-breakers if refused):**
1. Remove general data-room and public-register disclosure. Only specific, fair disclosure counts, and it never qualifies indemnities, fundamental warranties or tax.
2. Delete the Buyer-knowledge bar in cl 8.3, or confine it to actual knowledge of named individuals.
3. Limitations apply to general Warranty Claims only. Carve out fraud, fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities, covenants and leakage.
4. Fundamental warranties at 100% of price for 7+ years. Add a tax indemnity at 100% for 7 years.
5. Bluefen consent as a Buyer-only CP, unconditional and with all cl 11.3 conditions satisfied, with best endeavours, a long-stop date and a termination right.
6. Riverlark repaid at Completion from the price, with a payoff letter, releases and PPSR discharges delivered at Completion.
7. The DD-005 bonuses (AUD 420k) plus on-costs are deducted from the price and paid through payroll at Completion.

**Specific indemnities and retention:**
8. Ironquay: payment and confirmatory assignment pre-Completion, or a broad IP indemnity outside the cap.
9. DD-006: full incident file now, pre-Completion remediation covenant, and an uncapped or separately capped indemnity with a retention.
10. Escrow, retention or parent guarantee given the Seller's vehicle status. Consider W&I as the trade for the 20% cap.

**Negotiable economics:**
11. Tipping basket at ~AUD 120k (rather than a AUD 250k deductible) and de minimis at AUD 10–15k with aggregation. Hold the cap at 20% or tie it to W&I. General time limit 18–24 months.

**Diligence and follow-up:**
12. Sandbar contracts and approvals, possibly treated as leakage.
13. Independent title verification, including ASIC, PPSR and capitalisation table checks.
14. Lease notice and the Mossvale change-of-control check.
15. A bring-down of the Disclosure Letter dated 22 September, with no curing of breaches without Buyer consent.

**Process note:** given the improper AI-directed instruction embedded in the Disclosure Letter, consider asking Seller's counsel to confirm the final, authoritative version of SPA-003.

*The rates, periods and estimates above (superannuation guarantee, NSW payroll tax, NDB timing, ATO amendment periods) are working figures. NSW counsel and tax advisers should confirm them before we put them to the Seller.*
